raw_evidence: Calls have mounted for the deportation of Shabir Ahmed, who had dual British-Pakistani citizenship before being stripped of the former following his 2012 conviction for multiple counts of child sexual offences Ahmed, who was jailed for 22 years and released on licence this month, cannot be deported due to a 1971 law forbidding the removal of a small group of Commonwealth citizens who arrived in the UK more than 50 years ago Under the proposed amendment, foreign criminals will no longer benefit from these protections where they are guilty of some serious crimes It would bring the law on deportation in line with the law on the removal of citizenship Mahmood said the 1971 Act provided protections for long-term UK residents but "should not be used as a bar against removal in cases like that of Shabir Ahmed" But the Home Office said Ahmed's removal depends on Pakistan accepting him. At the moment, it appears Pakistan has no intention of accepting Ahmed, who claims to have renounced his Pakistani citizenship

He was subject to an Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) sentence, with no maximum term and is still serving his sentence But after the Prime Minister asked for a review of Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) sentences on Monday , his sister Pastor Clara White said there is now hope in sight "My brother doesn't know if he will ever leave prison or die there," Clara said. "It's inhumane. But the review brings a light in the darkness." Intended for the perpetrators of serious crimes and persistent criminals, Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) sentences were introduced in 2005. And allowed judges to give out sentences with no maximum tariff to perpetrators of serious crimes or repeat offenders Deemed controversial IPPs were scrapped in 2012, but this was not retrospective. As of this year, more than 2,000 people are still in prison on IPP sentences according to the United Nations, (UN), who have called for the end of IPP sentences. , external

Many people find themselves avoiding photographs, covering their mouth when they laugh, or struggling to enjoy their favourite foods. It's easy to believe these changes are simply something you have to live with Unfortunately, the effects of tooth loss don't stop there. Over time, the jawbone can begin to shrink and neighbouring teeth may come under additional strain, potentially leading to further problems. Fortunately, modern dentistry offers a solution that looks, feels and functions A dental implant is a small titanium replacement for the root of a missing tooth. Once healed, a bespoke crown is attached, creating a replacement tooth virtually indistinguishable from the real thing Unlike dentures, implants are fixed securely in place - no slipping, movement or adhesives required. Unlike traditional bridges, they don't rely on neighbouring healthy teeth for support, helping to preserve natural tooth structure
